title: Attention Is All You Need
tldr: Replaces recurrence and convolution entirely with (multi-head) self-attention, yielding a sequence-transduction architecture — the Transformer — that is more parallelizable, trains in a fraction of the time, and sets new single-model state of the art on WMT 2014 translation (28.4 BLEU EN–DE, 41.8 BLEU EN–FR).
contributions: The Transformer: an encoder–decoder architecture built solely from attention and position-wise feed-forward layers — no recurrence, no convolution (Figure 1)
Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention, with the 1/√d_k scaling justified by the growth of dot-product variance (Section 3.2, footnote 4)
State-of-the-art WMT 2014 results at a small fraction of prior training cost, plus generalization to English constituency parsing (Tables 2 and 4)
text: Sequence transduction in 2017 was dominated by recurrent encoder–decoders: the encoder walks the input one position at a time, so computation cannot be parallelized within a training example, and long-range dependencies must survive a chain of \(O(n)\) steps (Section 1). Attention had already proven useful for connecting encoder and decoder across arbitrary distances, but only as an add-on to a recurrent core. This paper removes the core. The Transformer keeps the encoder–decoder shape (Section 3, Figure 1) but builds both halves from just two ingredients: multi-head self-attention , which lets every position attend to every other position in one shot, and a position-wise feed-forward network . Order information, previously implicit in recurrence, is injected explicitly through sinusoidal positional encodings added to the embeddings (Section 3.5). The payoff is measured on WMT 2014 machine translation (Section 6.1, Table 2): the big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on English–German — more than 2 BLEU above the best previous results including ensembles — and 41.8 BLEU on English–French, a new single-model state of the art, after only 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs. The base model already beats all previously published single models at a training cost of \(3.3\times 10^{18}\) FLOPs, an order of magnitude below competitors. A 4-layer variant also generalizes to English constituency parsing with minimal tuning (Section 6.3, Table 4). The atom of the architecture is scaled dot-product attention (Section 3.2.1, Figure 2 left). Queries and keys of dimension \(d_k\) and values of dimension \(d_v\) are packed into matrices and combined as \[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V . \] The \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) factor is the paper's one delicate choice: if the components of \(q\) and \(k\) are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product \(q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i\) has variance \(d_k\) (footnote 4), so unscaled logits push the softmax into regions of vanishing gradient as \(d_k\) grows — which is exactly when additive attention otherwise wins (Section 3.2.1). Scaling restores the fast, matrix-multiply-friendly dot product. title: Multilayer Feedforward Networks are Universal Approximators
tldr: Single-hidden-layer feedforward networks with an arbitrary squashing activation can approximate any continuous function uniformly on compacta and any Borel measurable function in probability — so failures in practice must come from learning, too few hidden units, or noise, never from the architecture class itself.
contributions: Proves single-hidden-layer Σ networks with any squashing function are uniformly dense on compacta in C(R^r) and dense in probability in the Borel measurable functions (Theorem 2.4) — universality with no continuity assumption on the activation.
Establishes the same for ΣΠ networks with any continuous nonconstant activation via the Stone–Weierstrass theorem (Theorems 2.1–2.3).

Shows exact interpolation of any n distinct points by a single hidden layer with n units (Theorem 2.5), and extends universality to multi-output and deeper (l ≥ 2 layer) networks (Corollaries 2.6–2.7).

Frames what universality does and does not buy: nothing about how many hidden units are needed or whether weights can be learned — explicitly deferred to the sieve-estimation and metric-entropy literature.
text: By 1989, feedforward networks were succeeding across applications, but it was an open question whether this reflected a fundamental approximation capability or lucky problem selection. Minsky & Papert had killed the two-layer perceptron two decades earlier; the standing worry was that multilayer networks might also be limited to some special function class (§1). Kolmogorov's superposition theorem was often cited in the networks' defence, but it needs a different , unknown inner transformation for each target function, while practitioners use one fixed squashing nonlinearity (logistic, tanh) and simply add hidden units (§1). This paper settles the question. Using the Stone–Weierstrass theorem plus a constructive reduction through trigonometric polynomials and the Gallant–White "cosine squasher", it proves that a single hidden layer of squashing units — the activation can be any non-decreasing function from 0 to 1, continuous or not — makes the network class dense in the continuous functions (uniformly on every compact set) and dense in the Borel measurable functions in a probability metric, for every input dimension and every input distribution (Theorems 2.3–2.4, §2). The practical reading the authors themselves give (§3): when a network fails, the blame lies with inadequate learning, insufficient hidden units, or a stochastic input–target relation — never with the expressiveness of the architecture family. What the paper deliberately does not address is how many units a given accuracy costs, or how that count scales with input dimension — both flagged as open problems (§3). The objects are function classes built on affine maps. With \(A(x) = w \cdot x + b\) ranging over the affine functions \(\mathbf{A}^r\) (Def. 2.1), the single-hidden-layer class for an activation \(G\) is \[ \Sigma^r(G) = \Big\{ f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{q} \beta_j\, G(A_j(x)) : \beta_j \in \mathbb{R},\; A_j \in \mathbf{A}^r,\; q \in \mathbb{N} \Big\}, \] and \(\Sigma\Pi^r(G)\) additionally allows products \(\prod_{k} G(A_{jk}(x))\) inside each term (Defs. 2.2, 2.4).
